consensus_summary: The recognizable dominant Christian reading identifies lamp oil with the Holy Spirit or Spirit-given spiritual life, while common alternatives include readiness, inward grace or faith, good works, and the Word of God.
book_summary: The book identifies oil more specifically as divine commandment, truth, and correction received and stored inwardly until they produce proven obedience; the resulting light is that obedience visibly displayed to others.
rationale: The entry displaces the dominant equation of oil with the Holy Spirit, although it retains a Spirit-related dimension and combines several recognized minority readings: inward spiritual life, the Word or truth, and good works. Because those components are represented in the blind responses, the claim is not wholly novel, but its controlling identification is materially different from the common view.
strongest_objection: The interpretation depends on combining metaphors from separate passages: Psalm 141:5 calls reproof an excellent oil, Proverbs connects commandments with lamp and light, and Matthew connects visible light with good works, but Matthew 25 never identifies its oil as stored commandments or proven obedience. Zechariah 4 also more naturally supports the dominant Spirit reading.
